prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Prologis, Inc." (ticker PLD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PLD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Prologis, Inc.
result.industry: Industrial / logistics real estate investment trust (REIT)
markets: Logistics and distribution warehouses leased to retailers, e-commerce, 3PLs and manufacturers (US, Europe, Latin America, Asia)
Strategic capital: managing co-investment funds for institutional investors
Data center development on its land and power pipeline
Rooftop solar, battery storage and EV charging for customers (Prologis Energy)

mission.statement: Our people are the key to our success as we aspire to be the leading global real estate company as measured by customer service, employee engagement, financial performance and balance sheet strength.
mission.plain: Prologis wants to be the best real estate company in the world, judged by happy customers, engaged staff, strong profits and a strong balance sheet.

about.plain: Prologis owns huge warehouses near big cities around the world and rents them to companies that store and ship goods. It owns or manages about 1.3 billion square feet of buildings in 20 countries, with about 6,500 customers. It also builds new warehouses, runs investment funds that own warehouses together with big pension funds, and is starting to build data centers and solar power on its land.
about.customers: Online sellers, retailers, shipping and logistics companies and manufacturers that need space to store and move goods, such as Amazon and Home Depot.
about.everyday: A package you order online very often passes through a warehouse Prologis owns; Amazon is its largest customer with about 54 million square feet.

money.plain: Rent paid by companies using its buildings

money.part: Managing warehouse funds for investors (strategic capital)
money.plain: Asset management fees and performance promotes
Fees for building and managing projects for others
Powered sites and buildings for data centers; 5.8 GW power pipeline
Electricity from rooftop solar and batteries sold to customers and utilities

result.summary: Prologis has a durable, scale-based competitive advantage: it is by far the largest logistics landlord in the world (about 1.3 billion square feet in 20 countries) and its FY2025 revenue of $8.79 billion was about 73% of the combined revenue of the five largest US-listed industrial REITs. Its land bank and buildings in supply-constrained gateway markets, A-rated cheap capital, global customer relationships and its fund-management platform are very hard for rivals to replicate. The product itself (warehouse space) is a commodity, though, so its edge rests on location, scale and capital costs rather than on anything customers cannot get elsewhere.

pricingPower.evidence: In Q3 2026 new leases were signed at a 38.0% net effective rent increase (23.4% cash) over expiring leases while average occupancy held at 95.1% and retention was 75.9%; Q4 2025 net effective rent change was 43.8%, and cash same-store NOI growth guidance for 2026 was raised to 7.00%-7.50%.

moats.evidence: Ordinary people do not know the name, but among logistics customers and institutional investors Prologis is the default global brand, ranked first in real estate in Fortune's 2025 World's Most Admired Companies list.
Moving a distribution center means re-tooling automation and disrupting supply chains, which supports 75.9% retention in Q3 2026, but leases do expire and customers can move to rival buildings.
About 6,500 customers can expand across its 5,941 buildings in 20 countries, and it sells add-on services (energy, Essentials), but more customers do not directly make the product better for others.

With A2/A credit ratings, a 3.3% weighted average interest rate on its share of debt and about $8.8 billion of liquidity at September 30, 2026, it funds development and acquisitions far more cheaply than most rivals, and spreads overhead (G&A $469 million in FY2025) over $8.79 billion of revenue.

Its buildings cluster in land-constrained infill markets near big consumer populations where zoning and land scarcity limit new supply, though in many inland markets new warehouses can be built quickly.
Using its land and grid connections for data centers (5.8 GW power pipeline) and energy is an extension rivals can copy, not a model incumbents cannot adopt.

Decades of development experience (FY2026 development starts guided at $5.0-$5.75 billion at a 6.6% estimated yield in Q3 2026) and a proprietary data view across 1.3 billion square feet help it pick sites and price leases better than smaller rivals.

It owns irreplaceable land and buildings in gateway markets such as Southern California, New Jersey and around major European cities, plus secured power (1.7 GW) that newcomers would struggle to obtain.

customers.evidence: Retention was 75.9% in Q3 2026, occupancy averaged 95.1%, and a record 228 million square feet of leases was signed in 2025; the customer base is diversified, with Amazon the largest at only 5.6% of occupied space and Home Depot next at 1.7%. No NPS is published.

talent.evidence: Prologis cites a 4.7/5 Glassdoor rating with 96% of employees recommending it (February 2026), placement on U.S. News Best Companies to Work For 2025-2026 for a third straight year, and Fortune's World's Most Admired list for the fifth straight year in 2026.

product.evidence: Its portfolio is the largest and among the best-located in logistics real estate, it ranked first in real estate on Fortune's 2025 World's Most Admired list and appeared on the Corporate Knights Global 100 for the 16th time in 2026, and it adds services such as solar (536 MW operating solar and storage) and data center sites.

competitors.name: Blackstone (Link Logistics, BREIT and real estate funds)
competitors.note: Largest private owner of US warehouses through Link Logistics and its funds; competes for tenants, acquisitions and land in the US and Europe.

competitors.name: SEGRO plc
competitors.note: Leading UK and continental European logistics landlord; agreed in August 2026 to be acquired by Prologis for about $18.8 billion (closing expected 1H 2027).

competitors.name: Goodman Group
competitors.note: Global industrial property developer and fund manager in Asia-Pacific, Europe and the Americas, pivoting heavily to data centers.

competitors.name: Ares Management (GCP International, former GLP platform)
competitors.note: Owns and manages large logistics portfolios in the US, Europe, Japan and Brazil through the former GLP Capital Partners business and Ares Industrial REIT.

competitors.name: Panattoni
competitors.note: Private developer, one of the largest speculative and build-to-suit warehouse developers in Europe and the US.

competitors.name: Rexford Industrial Realty
competitors.note: Infill industrial REIT focused only on Southern California, Prologis's largest US market.

competitors.name: EastGroup Properties
competitors.note: Shallow-bay industrial buildings in Sunbelt markets such as Texas, Florida, Arizona and the Carolinas.

competitors.name: First Industrial Realty Trust
competitors.note: US bulk and regional warehouse REIT competing in many of the same coastal and inland markets.

competitors.name: STAG Industrial
competitors.note: Single-tenant US industrial buildings in secondary markets.

competitors.name: Terreno Realty
competitors.note: Infill industrial properties in six US coastal markets (New York/New Jersey, Los Angeles, Miami, San Francisco, Seattle, Washington DC).

competitors.name: CTP N.V.
competitors.note: Largest listed industrial developer-owner in Central and Eastern Europe.

competitors.name: ESR Group
competitors.note: Asia-Pacific logistics developer and fund manager (taken private in 2025); competes in Japan, China and Australia.

competitors.name: Brookfield Corporation (real estate funds)
competitors.note: Private real estate capital that owns and develops logistics portfolios globally.

competitors.name: LXP Industrial Trust
competitors.note: US warehouse REIT focused on Sunbelt and Midwest bulk distribution.

competitors.name: Digital Realty Trust
competitors.note: Competes with Prologis's new data center development business for powered sites and hyperscale customers.

estimates.name: Blackstone (Link Logistics, BREIT and real estate funds)
Ares Management (GCP International, former GLP platform)

marketShare.market: Share of combined FY2025 total revenues of the five largest US-listed industrial REITs (Prologis, Rexford, STAG, First Industrial, EastGroup), calculated from their 10-K filings and releases

threats: A new wave of speculative warehouse construction, or weaker demand from e-commerce and trade, could erode the large gap between in-place and market rents that drives its rent increases (net effective rent change 38.0% in Q3 2026).
Tariffs and trade disruption could slow leasing by importers, retailers and 3PLs that fill its port-adjacent buildings.
Higher interest rates raise the cost of its $36.8 billion of debt (September 30, 2026) and lower property values, which hurts development margins and fund-raising for strategic capital.
Integration and execution risk on the roughly $18.8 billion SEGRO acquisition, which management expects to be neutral to slightly dilutive to Core FFO in the first full year.
The data center push (5.8 GW power pipeline) needs large capital, power procurement and new skills, and competes with specialists such as Digital Realty and hyperscalers' own builds.
Large private capital (Blackstone, Ares/GCP, Brookfield) competing for the same assets and land, bidding up prices.

ceo.name: Daniel S. (Dan) Letter
ceo.background: BS in civil engineering from Marquette University; joined predecessor AMB Property in 2004 as a development manager in Chicago, later President of the US Central region, global head of capital deployment and President of Prologis before becoming CEO on January 1, 2026; co-founder Hamid Moghadam became executive chairman

c1.evidence: Prologis is the clear global leader in logistics real estate (about 1.3 billion square feet in 20 countries), but warehousing is a mature industry growing mid-to-high single digits (FY2025 revenue +7.2%), not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for well-located buildings in gateway markets, the ability to expand across 5,941 buildings in 20 countries and add-on services like solar and Essentials, and its land bank, A-rated capital and scale are very hard to replicate.

c3.evidence: It is the default leader among logistics customers and investors (first in real estate on Fortune's 2025 Most Admired list), but most ordinary people have never heard the name.

c4.evidence: Its published mission is to be 'the leading global real estate company' measured by customer service, employee engagement and financial results, which is professional and business-focused rather than an inspiring purpose.

c6.evidence: “warehouse landlord, Amazon's warehouses, blue-chip REIT” are typical associations among investors and logistics people, while the general public mostly does not know the name; the impression where it exists is positive.

c7.evidence: Logistics space is large and supported by e-commerce, supply-chain resilience and onshoring, and its data center power pipeline (5.8 GW) taps AI demand, but core warehouse demand grows modestly and is cyclical.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into data centers (1.7 GW secured power, 680 MW under development), energy (536 MW operating solar and storage), and Europe via the $18.8 billion SEGRO acquisition, using its land and customer relationships.

m1.evidence: Dan Letter, CEO since January 2026, has continued the strategy of extending logistics land into data centers and energy and struck the SEGRO deal, but his long-term vision is less established than founder Hamid Moghadam's.

m2.evidence: Letter is not a founder but a 22-year company veteran who started as a development manager in 2004; the co-founder remains executive chairman.

m4.evidence: Employee ratings are high (Glassdoor 4.7/5, 100% CEO approval as of February 2026), but there is little specific public evidence on Letter's personal leadership style so early in his tenure.

m5.evidence: The culture, built mainly under Moghadam, has added new businesses such as Prologis Essentials, energy and data centers, but it is a real estate company rather than a product inventor.

m6.evidence: Letter holds a civil engineering degree and spent years running development projects, so he is hands-on with the buildings, though not a technologist.

m7.evidence: No controversies are known and the company has long sustainability recognition (16 Corporate Knights Global 100 listings), but there is limited evidence about Letter's character beyond his corporate role.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Dan Letter at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Letter is a low-profile operator rather than a famous, distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2026, Core FFO guidance rose from $6.00-$6.20 to $6.25-$6.29 and quarterly results beat estimates, and before that he led capital deployment and the US Central region, but his CEO record is under a year long.

m10.evidence: G&A was $469 million or about 5.3% of FY2025 revenue on a $100+ billion balance sheet, which is efficient, but the company is not specifically known for frugality.

c10.evidence: Its warehouses help move everyday goods for about 6,500 customers in 20 countries, which indirectly benefits huge numbers of consumers, but it does not directly change lives the way a consumer product does.

p2.evidence: Assembling 1.3 billion square feet of well-located warehouses and land with power is very hard to replicate and important to supply chains, but building a single warehouse is not technologically hard.

f1.evidence: Total revenues rose every year from $4,439 million in FY2020 to $4,759 million, $5,974 million, $8,023 million, $8,202 million and $8,790 million in FY2025, and were up 8.8% in the first nine months of 2026.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin was 47.7% in FY2020 and 49.6% in FY2025 but swung between 46.2% and 67.4% with property-sale gains, so margins have not risen steadily.

f3.evidence: Debt of $36.8 billion far exceeds cash of $2.27 billion at September 30, 2026, but debt is only 23.9% of total market capitalization, debt/adjusted EBITDA is 4.5x, it is A-rated and equity is $60.3 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $2,119 million in FY2020 to $4,358 million in FY2025 and operating cash flow from $2,937 million to $5,008 million, though both dipped in one year (operating income in 2025, cash flow in 2024).

v1.evidence: It offers the largest choice of modern warehouses in the best logistics locations worldwide, a simple reason for big customers to choose it, but a nearby rival building can serve a customer just as well.

v2.evidence: It was on U.S. News Best Companies to Work For in 2025-2026 for the third straight year and Fortune's World's Most Admired list for the fifth straight year in 2026, and it reports a 4.7/5 Glassdoor rating.

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, retailers, 3PLs and Amazon would lose critical distribution space and its fund investors a manager, but the buildings would still exist under new owners, so consumers would barely notice.
